title: Ladders, elevated access and fall prevention
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: WorkSafe Victoria, High risk work licence (reviewed 30 June 2026); SafeWork NSW, High risk work licences (last modified 15 June 2026); SafeWork NSW, Working at heights (no visible date); WorkSafe Queensland, Boom type elevating work platform (WP) (no date shown).
audience: Handyman workers and property maintenance workers who may need to reach heights
learningOutcomes: Choose a ground-level or safer access method before a ladder is considered.
Judge whether a ladder is suitable for a task, including ground, weather and overhead conditions.
Identify the licence and duty boundaries for elevated work and refer tasks outside training or equipment limits.

instruction.heading: Ground-level methods come first
instruction.body: Before you choose a ladder, ask whether the work can be done from the ground, by reaching with a tool, or from a properly designed platform that is set up for the task. Many fixtures, gutters and fascia repairs can be reached without climbing. A ladder is a last-resort access method for short, low-risk tasks, and it is not a substitute for a platform when the task needs both hands, heavy material or sustained work. A short job does not make an unstable ladder acceptable.

instruction.heading: Judge the ladder and the setup
instruction.body: Check the ground condition. Soft, sloped, wet or uneven ground can make a ladder unstable, and a ladder should not be placed on loose material or on a surface that moves. Check the ladder itself for cracked rails, bent steps, missing feet and loose joints. Check the weather, because wind and rain change the risk. Check overhead hazards, including power lines and cables, before you lift a ladder. Do not work on a ladder when you cannot maintain three points of contact, and do not lean out beyond the belt line. If the task needs the top step or a step beyond the manufacturer's limit, the ladder is not suitable.

instruction.heading: Licence and duty boundaries for elevated work
instruction.body: In Victoria, operating a boom-type elevating work platform needs the WP licence class, and WorkSafe lists scissor lifts as outside the high risk licence requirement (WorkSafe Victoria page, reviewed 30 June 2026). Victoria's WP class sets no boom length. In New South Wales, the WP licence applies at a boom length of at least 11 metres, measured by the longer of two distances (SafeWork NSW licence page). A shorter boom may not need that licence there. In New South Wales, construction work that carries a fall risk above 2 metres needs a SWMS (SafeWork NSW working-at-heights page, no visible date; page metadata shows 21 October 2026). In Queensland, the WP licence covers boom-type platforms of 11 metres or more, and platforms under 11 metres fall outside that definition, so a shorter boom may not need the licence there (WorkSafe Queensland page, no date shown). These are statements of position for the licence classes and do not decide whether a specific handyman task is permitted. Refer any elevated task outside your training or equipment to a competent person.

procedure: Ask whether the task can be done from the ground or with a tool that reaches without climbing.
If access is needed, choose a platform or other method designed for the height and load before a ladder.
Check ground, weather and overhead hazards, including power lines and cables.
Inspect the ladder for defects and set it up according to the manufacturer instructions.
Maintain three points of contact and keep the body within the rails.
If the task cannot be done safely within the ladder or platform limit, stop and refer.

workedExamples.situation: A client asks you to repair an exterior fitting from the top step of a household ladder during light rain.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the task go ahead on the ladder as requested?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The top step is not a position a household ladder is designed to be used from, the rain makes the ladder and surfaces less stable, and the task is at height with an exterior fitting that may involve services. Decline the setup, isolate the area, and arrange a competent height-work assessment and suitable access. Record the decision and the reason.

equipmentAndPpe: Ladder inspected and set up to the manufacturer instructions
Non-slip footwear suited to the surface
Tool lanyard or tool bag for work at height
Barriers or signage for the area below

commonErrors.error: Using a ladder because the job looks short.
commonErrors.prevention: The length of a job does not change the risk. Choose access by the task and the conditions.

commonErrors.error: Standing on the top step or the top of a ladder not designed for it.
commonErrors.prevention: Follow the manufacturer's limits and do not exceed them.

commonErrors.error: Working from a ladder on uneven or wet ground.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, reset on stable ground, or choose a different access method.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Victoria: the WP class covers boom-type elevating work platforms (WorkSafe Victoria page, reviewed 30 June 2026). Victoria's WP class has no boom-length threshold, so the licence is not limited by length there. Scissor lifts sit outside the high risk licence requirement.

New South Wales: the WP licence applies at a boom length of at least 11 metres (SafeWork NSW licence page). A shorter boom may not need that licence in New South Wales. Construction work that carries a fall risk above 2 metres needs a SWMS (SafeWork NSW working-at-heights page, metadata date 21 October 2026).

Queensland: the WP licence covers boom-type platforms of 11 metres or more, and platforms under 11 metres fall outside that definition, so a shorter boom may not need the licence there (WorkSafe Queensland page, no date shown).
This lesson does not grant a high risk work licence or any authority to operate elevating work platforms.

qualityStandard: The access method is chosen and recorded before work starts, with the reason.
The ladder or platform is inspected and within its rated limits for the task.
Any elevated task outside training or equipment is referred and recorded.
documentationEvidence: Access decision record with the method chosen and the reason
Equipment inspection record for any ladder or platform used
Referral note for any elevated task declined
summary: Choose ground-level or platform methods before a ladder.
Check the ground, weather, overhead hazards and the ladder itself before climbing.
Licence positions for elevated plant are recorded by state, and this lesson grants none of them.

knowledgeChecks.question: A short fitting repair is needed at gutter height. What should you consider first?
options: Climb the household ladder because the job is short and the ladder is already set up and stable
Stand on the top step to reach it quickly, since it is the closest point to the work area
Check whether the task can be done from the ground or from a suitable platform before choosing a ladder
Lean out beyond the rails to avoid moving the ladder, since moving it wastes time on the job

knowledgeChecks.question: In Victoria, which statement about scissor lifts and the WP licence is correct according to the source?
options: Scissor lifts need the WP licence in all cases, whatever the height
Scissor lifts need the licence only over 11 metres in working height
WorkSafe states that scissor lifts do not need a high risk work licence
The source does not mention scissor lifts at all in its guidance

knowledgeChecks.question: Which condition makes a ladder unsuitable for use?
options: The ground is level and dry, and the ladder is tied off at the top so it can be used safely
The task is short, and the worker will be on the ladder for only a minute at most during the job
The worker has used the ladder before on many similar jobs in the past without any problem at all
The ground is soft or uneven, or the task needs the top step or a position beyond the manufacturer limit
